prose.text: Large language models have reshaped the relationship between people and computers. Users no longer need specialized syntax or commands; they can state what they want in ordinary language and receive responses that are coherent, contextually grounded, and often genuinely useful.

Yet the dominant interface for these models remains the chatbot, a medium organized around sequential turns of conversation. Users are required to translate what they want into explicit natural-language requests, then mentally track how each new output differs from the last.

Conversation, however, is a poor fit for the act of writing. Writers think through revision by acting on text directly, moving sentences, cutting phrases, and reshaping structure, not by formulating verbal instructions and waiting for a response.

Our system moves away from conversational revision toward direct manipulation of the document itself. Writers can select any passage to browse alternative phrasings, or drag sections into a new order when the structure feels wrong. The system surfaces editorial feedback as inline annotations anchored to specific spans of text, so writers see exactly what changed and why, rather than discovering a silently rewritten draft.
